beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Every AI user discovers this trick sooner or later: before your question, you tell the AI who to be. Act as a chef. Act as an expert editor. Act as a patient tutor. And the answers come out different. So this film is about what that one line is really doing — and when it's worth typing.

beats.narration_text: Three terms for this film. A role prompt: a line at the start of your prompt that gives the AI a job to act as. Register: how an answer is pitched — its words, what it assumes you know, its tone, and how deep it goes. And a persona: a whole invented character with a voice of its own.

beats.narration_text: The trick is one line at the start of your prompt. Act as a chef. That line has a name: a role prompt. It doesn't change what you asked for — you still want a lemon pasta recipe. It changes who you're asking.

beats.narration_text: Now, the role is not a costume. Think of it as four dials: the words it picks, what it assumes you already know, how formal its tone is, and how deep it goes. The moment a role lands, all four dials turn at once. The AI doesn't become a chef, and it doesn't believe it's one. Those four dials together are called the register — and a role calibrates the register.

beats.narration_text: Watch the dials move. The role lands — act as a patient tutor — and all four dials swing: words toward simple, knowledge toward nothing-assumed, tone warmer, depth shorter. Same question in, a different answer out, and nobody added any facts. The role only set the register.

beats.narration_text: Now the classic experiment. Ask two doctors the same question. The pediatric oncologist is talking to a child: simple words, nothing assumed, warm, and short. The pathologist is presenting at grand rounds: technical, precise, and deep. Same facts, same question — two completely different answers. The role added no facts. It only set the register.

beats.narration_text: A role is small and functional: you are an expert tax attorney. A persona is the whole costume: you are Marcus, a sardonic nineteen-seventies tax attorney who speaks in nautical metaphors. The role calibrates the answer. The persona adds a character with a voice. Both are valid tools — a role tunes the register, a persona adds the voice. Know which one you need.

beats.narration_text: When is the line worth typing? Two piles. Feedback, explaining, advice — here the audience decides what's good, so set the role. Extracting a date, doing a sum — the job doesn't care about register, so the role adds nothing. The test is simple: does the role change what counts as a good answer? If it can't change what good looks like, skip it.

beats.narration_text: One last tip. 'Act as a genius' is vague — and a vague role calibrates nothing. Make the role specific instead, and give it an audience: 'act as a patient math tutor for a ten-year-old.' Say the job, say who it's for, and put the line first.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Ask one question twice. First, start it with: act as an expert explaining to a curious beginner. Then ask the same question again, starting with: act as an expert explaining to a fellow expert. Put the two answers side by side. Then check two things yourself. Can you point to three words that appear in only one of the two answers? And which answer was actually more useful to you — and why?
